# Evaluations, Arize & Phoenix Observability in `twyne`

## 1. Arize / Phoenix instrumentation & OTLP tracing

**`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/convex/arizeTracing.ts`** — the single instrumentation entry point. It:
- Uses `@arizeai/openinference-vercel` (`OpenInferenceSimpleSpanProcessor`, `isOpenInferenceSpan`) plus `@opentelemetry/*` (`NodeTracerProvider`, `OTLPTraceExporter` proto exporter, `resourceFromAttributes`).
- Is **dormant-when-unconfigured**: `tracingEnabled = Boolean(ARIZE_API_KEY && ARIZE_SPACE_ID)`. Without creds it registers no provider and `flushArize()` is a no-op (mirrors `convex/posthog.ts`).
- Uses a **simple/synchronous span processor** (not batch) because Convex "use node" actions are short-lived serverless and could drop batched spans when the runtime freezes.
- Sends OTLP to a **region-sharded** endpoint: `https://otlp.${ARIZE_REGION}.arize.com/v1/traces` (default region `ca-central-1a`), auth via `arize-space-id` + `arize-api-key` **headers** (not bearer). Resource attributes set `model_id` = project name, `model_version` = "1.0.0".
- Exports `tracingEnabled` and `flushArize()`.

**`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/convex/agents.ts`** — the production consumer:
- Imports the tracer for side-effect registration (`import "./arizeTracing"`) and pulls in `tracingEnabled` + `flushArize`.
- Feeds the Vercel AI SDK's `experimental_telemetry` block on every `generateText` call (`isEnabled: tracingEnabled`, `functionId: feature`, metadata: feature/persona/provider/model). The AI SDK emits OTel spans that the OpenInference processor transforms into Arize/Phoenix-compatible LLM spans.
- Calls `await flushArize()` before each action returns (many call sites, e.g. lines ~239, 258, 301, 563, 785, 1576).

No standalone Phoenix server/collector config exists — "Phoenix" appears only as the OpenInference span convention (Arize AX is the backend). Package deps confirming this are in **`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/package.json`** (`@arizeai/openinference-vercel`, `@opentelemetry/api`, `exporter-trace-otlp-proto`, `resources`, `sdk-trace-node`).

## 2. What evaluations exist & how they run

All evals live in **`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/evals/`** and are **offline harnesses run via npm scripts** (defined in `package.json` lines 49-54). They do **not** need Arize creds — they call the **Bifrost** OpenAI-compatible gateway directly with header-only auth (`x-bifrost-api-key`, never `Authorization: Bearer`, which Bifrost misreads as a virtual-key lookup → 401).

| npm script | Runner file | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `npm run eval` | `run-experiment.ts` | Replays `dataset.jsonl` through the **real production prompt builders** (`convex/agentPrompts` → `buildSystemPrompt`/`buildUserPrompt`, personas from `src/utils/personas`); writes `runs.json` in the shape `ax experiments create --file` accepts. |
| `npm run eval:judge` | `judge.ts` | **LLM-as-judge**: scores `runs.json` on two rubrics → `scores.json`. |
| `npm run eval:rubric` | `run-rubric.ts` | Replays real prompts for 4 task types (rubric-judge/review/evidence/integrity); LLM-as-judge → `rubric-scores.json`. |
| `npm run eval:apparatus` | `run-apparatus.ts` | Runs `apparatus.jsonl` → `apparatus-scores.json`. |
| `npm run eval:interview` | `run-interview.ts` | Replays interview conversations `interview.jsonl` through the production interview agent → `interview-scores.json`. |
| `npm run eval:robustness` | `run-robustness.ts` | Robustness suite → `robustness-scores.json`. |

**The two LLM-as-judge rubrics** (in `judge.ts`) explicitly mirror, verbatim, two Arize template evaluators created under the "kmannoel Space":
- **faithfulness-to-draft** — does feedback engage THIS specific draft (`grounded`=1) vs. generic boilerplate (`generic`=0)?
- **feedback-helpfulness** — is feedback useful + on-persona (`good`=1) vs. vague/off-topic (`poor`=0)?

Judge runs at temperature 0, returns strict JSON `{label, explanation}`, default judge model `neuralwatt/kimi-k2.6` (override with `JUDGE_MODEL`). A key documented rationale: the **native Arize judge task is blocked** because the AI-integration injects `Authorization: Bearer` to Bifrost → 401; this in-repo script reproduces the same rubrics with header-only auth so evals are reproducible in CI. (This implies the Arize integration `auth_type` must be `proxy_with_headers`.)

**Where results go:** all scores are written as JSON files committed into `evals/` (`scores.json`, `rubric-scores.json`, `interview-scores.json`, `apparatus-scores.json`, `robustness-scores.json`, plus `runs.json`). `scores.json` shape: array of `{case_id, persona, faithfulness{label,score,explanation}, helpfulness{...}}`.

**CI:** `/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/.github/workflows/ci.yml` delegates entirely to a **Dagger** pipeline (`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/.dagger/src/index.ts`) doing "lint · typecheck · test · build · package". I found **no eval invocation in CI or the Dagger pipeline** — evals are run manually/locally despite the "reproducible in CI" comment. Note: `evals/upload-experiment.ts` is referenced in `run-experiment.ts` comments (join case_id→Arize example_id) but **does not exist** in the repo.

## 3. Environment variables / config (names only)

Documented in **`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/.env.example`** (set in Convex deployment env per the notes):
- Arize (observability): `ARIZE_API_KEY`, `ARIZE_SPACE_ID`, `ARIZE_PROJECT_NAME` (default `twyne`), `ARIZE_REGION` (default `ca-central-1a`; options us-east-1b / us-central-1a / eu-west-1a / ca-central-1a), `ARIZE_OTLP_ENDPOINT` (optional full URL override).
- Eval harness (Bifrost gateway): `BIFROST_BASE_URL`, `BIFROST_API_KEY`, `BIFROST_DEFAULT_MODEL` (default `neuralwatt/qwen3.5-397b-fast`), `JUDGE_MODEL` (default `neuralwatt/kimi-k2.6`).
- PostHog-based AI eval capture (parallel observability path): `POSTHOG_PROJECT_API_KEY`, `POSTHOG_HOST`, `POSTHOG_CAPTURE`, plus client `PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY`/`PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST`/`PUBLIC_POSTHOG_CAPTURE`.

## 4. Docs / notes

There is **no dedicated eval doc** (no `evals/README.md`). The authoritative documentation is:
- The **`.env.example` "Arize (LLM observability + evals)" section** (lines 59-84) — the clearest prose description of how the whole harness fits together.
- **Docstring headers** at the top of each `evals/*.ts` file (esp. `run-experiment.ts` and `judge.ts`) — they describe intent, the Bifrost auth gotcha, the Arize-integration 401 rationale, and output paths.
- **`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`** and `docs/growth-strategy.md` exist but were not eval-focused in the scan.

## How the pieces connect

Two independent observability paths plus an offline harness:

1. **Live tracing → Arize AX:** production `convex/agents.ts` `generateText` calls emit AI-SDK telemetry → `arizeTracing.ts` OpenInference processor → OTLP (region-sharded, header auth) → Arize project "twyne" in the kmannoel Space. Gated on `ARIZE_*` creds.
2. **Live capture → PostHog:** `src/utils/ai-evals.ts` (`captureAiGeneration`) + `convex` `captureServerAiGeneration` push generation events (clamped text, trace ids, eval signals) to PostHog for its AI-eval product. Gated on `POSTHOG_*`.
3. **Offline harness (repo/CI-friendly):** npm `eval:*` scripts replay committed `*.jsonl` datasets through the *real* production prompt builders via Bifrost, then LLM-as-judge scorers (rubrics that duplicate the Arize evaluators) write JSON score files into `evals/`. This exists precisely because the native Arize judge integration is blocked by the Bearer-auth 401 issue.

## Portkey Hosted Gateway: Required Headers

**Base URL:** `https://api.portkey.ai/v1` (chat completions endpoint: `https://api.portkey.ai/v1/chat/completions`)

### Required headers

1. **`x-portkey-api-key`** — Always required. This is your Portkey account's API key, obtained from the Portkey dashboard (env var: `PORTKEY_API_KEY`). It authenticates you *to Portkey itself*.

2. **Provider auth** — Required, via one of four mechanisms:

   - **Provider slug + Authorization**: Set `x-portkey-provider` to a raw slug (e.g., `openai`, `anthropic`) and pass the upstream key as `Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN`. Useful when you don't want keys stored in Portkey's vault.
   - **AI Provider (Model Catalog)**: Set `x-portkey-provider` using the `@provider-slug` format (e.g., `@openai-prod`). The upstream key is managed in Portkey's Model Catalog, so no `Authorization` header is needed. Note: "`x-portkey-virtual-key` / `virtual_key` / `virtualKey` parameter is the legacy equivalent and still works for backward compatibility."
   - **Config**: `x-portkey-config` accepts a saved config ID or inline JSON containing provider details (also enables caching, load balancing, fallbacks, retries, timeouts).
   - **Custom Host**: `x-portkey-custom-host` points at your own base URL (e.g., a self-hosted or OpenAI-compatible endpoint). Portkey "blocks private/reserved IP ranges by default." You must also set `x-portkey-provider` — the docs say if unsure, "you can set `openai`" — plus `Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN` for that upstream.

### How Authorization works for OpenAI-compatible custom providers

Portkey normalizes auth formats: you always send `Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN`, and if the upstream expects `x-api-key` or `api-key` instead, Portkey converts it into the provider-specific format automatically.

### Minimal example (custom host, OpenAI-compatible)

```sh
curl https://api.portkey.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "x-portkey-api-key: $PORTKEY_API_KEY" \
  -H "x-portkey-custom-host: https://your-host/v1" \
  -H "x-portkey-provider: openai" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Optional extras include `x-portkey-trace-id`, `x-portkey-metadata`, `x-portkey-cache-force-refresh`, `x-portkey-request-timeout`, and `x-portkey-forward-headers` for passing sensitive headers upstream untouched.

One note on your context: your Portkey and model API keys live in your skate/Railway secret stores — reference them via environment variables rather than embedding them in code or configs.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Here's what I found about the Portkey Admin API's Create Integration endpoint and custom host support:

## Create Integration Endpoint

The endpoint is documented at Portkey's Admin API docs (control plane): **POST** `https://api.portkey.ai/v1/integrations` (or your `SELF_HOSTED_CONTROL_PLANE_URL`). It requires an `x-portkey-api-key` header, and the JSON body has required fields: `name` (human-readable name, e.g. "Production OpenAI") and `ai_provider_id` (ID of the base AI provider, e.g. "openai"), plus an optional `slug` (URL-friendly identifier, auto-generated if not provided, pattern `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`).

Example via the Python SDK:
```python
from portkey_ai import Portkey
portkey = Portkey(api_key="PORTKEY_API_KEY")
integration = portkey.integrations.create(
    name="openai-production",
    ai_provider_id="openai",
    key="sk-..."
)
```
A successful 200 response returns the integration's `id` and `slug`.

Additional options: You can control whether to automatically create a default provider when creating a workspace-scoped integration (defaults to true), and supply a custom slug for the auto-created default provider — only applicable for workspace-scoped integrations; if the slug already exists in the workspace, the request fails with a validation error. The API also supports dynamically resolving secrets from secret references at runtime.

Related endpoints include List Integrations (GET), Retrieve Integration (GET), Update Integration (PUT), Delete Integration (DEL), plus Model Access and Workspace Access sub-resources.

## Custom Host / Self-Hosted Providers

For privately hosted models, when creating a new integration, you enable the "Local/Privately hosted provider" toggle, select the API specification your LLM implements (e.g., OpenAI), enter your model's base URL in the "Custom Host" field, and add any required authentication headers — allowing self-hosted models to work with all Portkey features.

Key custom host detail: the `custom_host` must include the API version path (e.g., `/v1/`); Portkey automatically appends the endpoint path (`/chat/completions`, `/completions`, or `/embeddings`). Also note Portkey blocks requests to private and reserved IP ranges by default to prevent SSRF attacks; routing to a private network IP requires allowlisting specific hosts.

## Model Catalog Relationship

In Portkey, stored credentials are called Integrations — a secure vault for API keys — and once you create an Integration, you can use it to create multiple AI Providers. Creating credentials in the Model Catalog automatically creates a workspace-linked integration; to share credentials across multiple workspaces, create them via the Integrations page (org admin only). There's also a Terraform provider that manages Portkey resources through the Portkey Admin API, including organization-level AI provider integrations.

Auth: header `x-portkey-api-key` (security scheme `Portkey-Key`, `type: apiKey, in: header`). The spec doesn't explicitly state which key type/permission is needed, but since integrations are org/workspace admin resources and `workspace_id` is a body field, this is an admin-level operation on the control plane (`https://api.portkey.ai/v1` or your `SELF_HOSTED_CONTROL_PLANE_URL`).

## Top-level fields (`CreateIntegrationRequest`)

**Required:** `name`, `ai_provider_id`

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | "Human-readable name for the integration" |
| `ai_provider_id` | string | "ID of the base AI provider", e.g. `openai` |
| `slug` | string | pattern `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`; auto-generated if omitted |
| `key` | string | "API key for the provider (if required)" |
| `description` | string | optional |
| `workspace_id` | string | "Workspace ID (for workspace-scoped integrations)", e.g. `ws-my-team-1234` |
| `configurations` | object | provider-specific; `oneOf` the schemas below |
| `create_default_provider` | boolean | default `true`; auto-creates a default provider for workspace-scoped integrations |
| `default_provider_slug` | string | pattern `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`, max 255; fails validation if slug already exists in workspace |
| `secret_mappings` | array of SecretMapping | runtime secret resolution; each `target_field` must be unique; if `key` is mapped, the `key` body field may be omitted |
| `pricing_adjustments` | object (nullable) | `{ "multiplier": PricingMultiplier }` |

## `configurations` variants (oneOf)

- **OpenAIConfiguration**: `openai_organization`, `openai_project`
- **AzureOpenAIConfiguration** (req: `azure_resource_name`, `azure_deployment_config`, `azure_auth_mode` ∈ default/entra/managed): plus `azure_entra_tenant_id`, `azure_entra_client_id`, `azure_entra_client_secret`, `azure_managed_client_id`. - **AzureAIConfiguration** (req: `azure_foundry_url`, `azure_auth_mode`): `azure_api_version`, `azure_deployment_name`, entra/managed fields as above
- **WorkersAIConfiguration** (req: `workers_ai_account_id`)

- **HuggingFaceConfiguration**: `huggingface_base_url`
- **CortexConfiguration** (req: `snowflake_account`)
- **CustomHostConfiguration** ← this is the custom base URL option:
  - `custom_host` — "Custom host URL (can be used along with other provider specific configuration fields)"

- `secret_reference_id` (req) — UUID or slug of the secret reference
